cards.explanation: The answer is that their fathers told them. Asaph says these are things “…that we have heard and known and our fathers have relayed to us.” So this wasn't a secret anybody dug up in the attic. It was handed down, mouth to ear, like a family recipe nobody ever wrote down. Somebody's dad said it, and somebody's kid remembered it.

The answer is False. Asaph says, “We will not hide them from their children…” Instead they will declare to the next generation the praises of the LORD, His might and the wonders He has performed. These stories are for sharing, loudly, friends. Nobody's keeping this one a secret.

The answer is so they'd put their confidence in God. Asaph says it right there: “…that they should put their confidence in God, not forgetting His works, but keeping His commandments.” Every generation hears the stories so they remember what God has done. Remembering is how you lean on Him, friends. That's the whole point of the relay.

The answer is stubborn and rebellious. That's Asaph's word for the fathers: “…a stubborn and rebellious generation, whose heart was not loyal, whose spirit was not faithful to God.” Asaph doesn't sugarcoat it. He wants the next generation to hear it plainly so they can choose differently. Stubborn is a hard word, but it's the one he picked.
The answer is True. Asaph follows it up fast. Right after the archers of Ephraim turn back, he says they “…refused to live by His law.” He also says they didn't keep God's covenant.

The answer is forgot. Asaph says, “They forgot what He had done, the wonders He had shown them.” Forgetting is the heart of this whole psalm. I know a little about being forgotten, friends, and I wouldn't wish it on a wonder. That's why the stories keep getting passed down.

The answer is False. There's no sun and no drying up in Asaph's telling. He says, “He split the sea and brought them through; He set the waters upright like a wall.” God split it, and the waters stood up. That's a different kind of wonder altogether.

The answer is a cloud by day and fire by night. Asaph says, “He led them with a cloud by day and with a light of fire all night.” A cloud by day and a light of fire all night. Day and night, God covered the whole shift.

The answer is water. Asaph says God “…split the rocks in the wilderness and gave them drink as abundant as the seas.” Then he adds, “He brought streams from the stone and made water flow down like rivers.” A rock, in the middle of a wilderness, pouring out rivers. I'd have stared at it for a week.

The answer is demanding. Asaph says, “They willfully tested God by demanding the food they craved.” The word is demanding, and it's not the same as asking. They were putting God to the test on purpose. That's a different thing than a hungry heart saying, 'Lord, we need help.'

The answer is that He can give bread or meat. The people say, “When He struck the rock, water gushed out and torrents raged. But can He also give bread or supply His people with meat?” They mention the water, then ask about bread and meat. I think that question is where the doubt shows.

The answer is wrath. Asaph says, “Therefore the LORD heard and was filled with wrath; so a fire was kindled against Jacob, and His anger flared against Israel…” The LORD heard what they said. Asaph gives the reason: “…they did not believe God or rely on His salvation.”

The answer is True. Asaph says it plainly. God's anger flared “…because they did not believe God or rely on His salvation.” The problem was a heart that wouldn't trust Him. That's the reason the verse gives.
The answer is manna. Asaph says, “He rained down manna for them to eat; He gave them grain from heaven.” The doors of the heavens open, and food comes down. Manna is the food he names.

The answer is birds. Asaph says, “He rained meat on them like dust, and winged birds like the sand of the sea.” That's a lot of birds, friends. Right before it, he says God stirred the east wind and drove the south wind by His might.

The answer is False. The verse says, “He felled them in the midst of their camp, all around their dwellings.” So it happened in the middle of the camp, around where the people lived. Not out in the distance.
The answer is seek. Asaph says, “When He slew them, they would seek Him; they repented and searched for God.” Hard times pointed them back toward God. Searching is what the verse says they did.

The answer is False. Asaph says, “Their hearts were disloyal to Him, and they were unfaithful to His covenant.” Just before that, he says they deceived Him with their mouths and lied to Him with their tongues. The words sounded good, but the hearts weren't loyal.

The answer is that God forgives them and spares them. Asaph says, “And yet He was compassionate; He forgave their iniquity and did not destroy them.” The hearts were disloyal, and still God was compassionate. I know what it is to be handed grace I didn't earn, friends.

The answer is True. It's a gentle line in a hard story. Asaph says, “He often restrained His anger and did not unleash His full wrath.” Often, he says, not once. That tells me something about the heart of God.

The answer is that they were only flesh. Asaph says, “He remembered that they were but flesh, a passing breeze that does not return.” God knew exactly what they were made of. And no, that's not an excuse, it's what the verse says He remembered.
